Hi Baljeet,

Thanks for joining the outage review yesterday. Last week we'd said it was one person's slip; this time we went back and asked properly. I've written it up since you're travelling. The site went down after Tuesday's release. Why? A bad setting reached the live site. Why? The deployment doesn't check settings before going out. Why? The check sat on an old list nobody updated. Why? Nobody owned that list after the team changed. Why did it matter? Nothing else would have caught it. We didn't name a person, only a gap. So we've added an automated test that fails the release if a setting is missing, and the list now has an owner each quarter. Could you look over the wording of the test?

Tanuja

qa.a: The team added an automated test that fails the release if a setting is missing.

qa.a: The team could rehearse a quick rollback of a bad release, since a fast way back limits the damage when a check still misses something.

qa.a: Baljeet probably feels included and trusted, since Tanuja wrote it up for someone travelling and asked for help with the test wording.

Chetan, you were on leave during the outage review, so let Payal tell you what happened, because I think we finally did it right.
Last time, we blamed Suresh and moved on, and it happened again. This time I said, nobody's name goes on the board till we've asked why five times.
Why did the site go down? A bad config went live. Why did it go live? It passed review. Why did review pass it? The reviewer only saw the code diff, not the config. Why? Because config changes aren't shown in review at all. Why? Because our deployment script never included them.
So the cause wasn't a person. It was a gap in our process.
We added an automatic check that stops any deployment if the config fails a test. Suresh wrote it himself, actually. Two months now. No repeat.

qa.q: How might Payal feel about this outage review compared with the last one?
qa.a: Payal seems relieved and quietly proud, believing the team finally did it right by finding a process gap instead of blaming someone.

qa.q: What else could the team add to keep this from recurring, and why?
qa.a: They could review other steps in the deployment script for similar gaps, since one missing check suggests there may be others.

qa.q: How might Suresh see the new review?
qa.a: Suresh, who was blamed last time, may feel respected and relieved, and writing the fix himself suggests he felt trusted.

grounding: It shows a team revisiting an outage, asking why five times until they find a missing deployment check, and adding an automated test instead of assigning blame.

passage:
I'm Farhan, and I'm new in the QA team, so I mostly sat and watched Ishita's outage review on Thursday.
I'd heard the last one had ended in five minutes with somebody blamed. This time Ishita put a rule on the board first: "No names. Just why."
Then she kept asking. Why did the orders stop? The database connection broke. Why? A setting was changed. Why wasn't it caught? The test suite doesn't cover settings. Why? Nobody owned that part. Why? It was never on anyone's checklist.
It took forty minutes. People kept wanting to say who did it, and she kept pulling them back to why.
At the end, she assigned an automatic settings test to be added to every deployment, and put a name next to the task, not next to the mistake.
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked tired but satisfied.

qa.q: How long did Ishita's outage review take?
What does Ishita looking tired but satisfied suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ishita felt worn out but content, having kept the team on process instead of blame, though Farhan can't be certain.

qa.q: What else could Ishita do with what the review found, and why?
qa.a: She could share the five whys with other teams, since a missing checklist item may affect their deployments too.

qa.q: How might the person who changed the setting experience this review?
qa.a: They may feel relieved and safer, since the review pointed at a missing test instead of at them.

grounding: It shows a team asking why five times after an outage until a process gap appears, and adding an automated test rather than blaming someone.
